extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on news recommendation systems (NRS), including recommender-system engineers and academics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and quality criteria for news recommender systems (NRS), covering both accuracy and beyond-accuracy metrics, news-specific evaluation protocols, datasets, and conventional solutions to core NRS challenges (timeliness, user modeling, content quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures the degree of 'dissimilarity' among the recommended items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically implemented through re-ranking of recommendation lists. Well-known metrics include Intra-List Similarity (ILS) (pairwise similarity among recommended items), temporal (Lathia's) diversity (diversity across sequences of recommendation lists over time), normalized diversity, and others (see Kunaver and Porl 2017). ILS can be computed over items, topics, categories, tags, or sentiments (tone). Computing ILS per individual user is computationally expensive at NRS scale; research needed on level of diversification and scalability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents the percentage of distinct items/users/ratings that a recommender system can recommend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common interpretations: item coverage (percentage of items recommended), user coverage (percentage of users covered), catalog coverage (percentage of recommended user-item pairs), and interaction coverage (rating predictions) over potential items/users/user-item pairs/ratings. In the news domain coverage is often used to determine topical coverage (e.g., number of user visits over time). Research on coverage in NRS is limited and mostly focuses on item coverage; coverage relates to not only recommended items but the whole NRS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Determines how different or unknown a recommendation is relative to what has been previously recommended to a user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty may be defined at three levels: life-level (user has never heard of the item in their life), system-level (item is unknown to the user per their consumption history), and recommendation-level (non-redundant item in the recommendation list). In NRS novelty is challenging because much in news is inherently new. Simple operationalization: inverse of popularity or ratio of unknown items in top-N. Novelty research in NRS has mostly been at item level; it should also cover overall content, events, and uniqueness of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serendipity
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite concept including relevance (usefulness), novelty (newness) and unexpectedness (surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from novelty: a novel item is unfamiliar, but serendipitous items are unexpected and valuable/interesting to the user (e.g., change attitude). Some NRS define serendipity as composed of accuracy, novelty and diversity; others define it in terms of semantically related yet unexpected topics. Research is limited because serendipity has many combinatory definitions, complicating evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective user experience / user satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: User experience is a subjective, multifaceted concept affecting satisfaction before, during, and after recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common evaluation approaches: (i) user studies with questionnaires at different recommendation stages, (ii) combine longitudinal logged data with questionnaires, (iii) combine accuracy and beyond-accuracy metrics. Knijnenburg et al. (2012) propose a user experience framework with six components: objective system aspects (algorithm, presentation, interface, features), user experience (user choices/evaluations), perception/subjective aspects (user evaluation of objective aspects), situational (context like social, trust, goal), personal characteristics (gender, location), and objective interaction (observable behavior: browsing, viewing, sign-ins, ratings). NRS-specific small frameworks: Asikin & Wörndl use three factors (appropriate, like, surprising); Constantinides & Dowell use six factors (reading frequency, reading time, time of day, reading style, browsing strategy, location). Researchers sometimes equate satisfaction with accuracy, but others link it to beyond-accuracy aspects like serendipity or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional predictive correctness measures (precision, recall, NDCG, MRR, AUC, HR, CTR, RMSE, etc.) assessing how well recommendations match user preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is the most widely used evaluation measure in NRS research. It is often used alongside or traded off with beyond-accuracy metrics (diversity, novelty). Many papers use offline protocols and standard IR/RS metrics (prec, rec, F1, AUC, NDCG, MRR, CTR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-List Similarity (ILS) and other diversity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairwise diversity metric commonly used to evaluate diversity in recommendation lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ILS computes similarity between any two items in a recommended list; remains popular in NRS. Other diversity metrics include temporal/Lathia's diversity (over time) and normalized diversity. ILS can be applied to items, topics, categories, tags, or sentiments; computational cost at scale is an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized @k (popularity-bias mitigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A personalized @k metric that removes k popular items from the recommendation list to reduce popularity bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed to eliminate popularity bias caused by datasets/websites that automatically surface popular items; removes k most popular items to compute performance on less-popular recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saliency (news-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saliency metric measuring importance of named entities in news articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saliency computed as a function of entity frequency with a decay factor based on distance of the first occurrence position in text. Motivated by news discourse structure where key facts/entities appear in early paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-impact (news-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric trading off recency and importance to identify high-impact news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines recency (age after publication) and relevance/importance; recently published stories often have higher future-impact scores. Used to rank or prioritize potentially high-impact stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff metric (accuracy vs diversity/novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metric designed to balance high accuracy (precision/recall) with reasonable diversity and novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes higher accuracy improves personalization and reader experience, while reasonable diversity prevents boredom. Designed to keep readers engaged while ensuring diverse recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senti (sentiment diversity metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metric evaluating sentiment diversity of recommended news using normalized MRR and hit ratio scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senti is positive if the top-ranked news has the same sentiment orientation as the overall sentiment; higher values when sentiments are stronger. Intended to capture sentiment diversity/orientation in top recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocols (offline, online, user studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental settings used to measure recommendation quality: offline simulation/experimentation, online experiments (A/B or real-time), and user studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offline evaluation is most widely used in NRS research (cheaper). Online evaluation and user studies are more expensive but provide real-world/user-facing signals. Distribution in surveyed literature: many offline papers, fewer online and user studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (news-specific challenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to recommend timely, fresh, and low-latency items — early reporting is more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics to factor: popularity, recency, freshness, trends, uniqueness, and low latency. CLEF NEWSREEL working notes: a well-formed recommendation must respond within a given time frame (100 ms). Timeliness requires real-time processing and computational efficiency for large numbers of articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-decay models (for timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation algorithms that give more weight to recent items using time-sensitive weighting or sliding/adaptive windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sliding/timing windows consider recent items and discard or downweight older data. Window size should be adaptive: large windows can cause concept drift; small windows may lack sufficient data to learn short-term preferences. Effective short-term preference modeling is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-based solutions for timeliness/sequential modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph-based models that represent relationships and sequential reading behavior to predict next-news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Context Trees (anonymous readers), Browse-Graphs, Markov decision processes. These models capture sequential dependencies but may suffer from state explosion and may fail to capture complex patterns at large scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity-based solutions and their pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Models ranking by popularity (clicks, visit counts, social signals) used as a baseline for news recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple popularity counting is easy but prone to amplification/popularity bias (hard top-N cutoffs penalize near-top candidates). Mitigation: probabilistic selection proportional to current popularity (feedback loops). Popularity signals from social networks or trends may help, but popularity does not guarantee credibility (false news can be more popular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs implicit feedback (user modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary sources of feedback: explicit (ratings) and implicit (clicks, browsing, reading time, scroll percentage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In NRS explicit ratings are often missing; implicit signals (clicks, reading time, scroll %) are used as proxies for interest. Consider how to interpret and incorporate these signals for modeling user preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: User modeling considerations (anonymous readers, profiling, passive consumption, negative feedback, intent relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects to consider when modeling users in NRS: anonymous users, registered user profiles, passive consumption behaviors, negative implicit feedbacks, and relevance of readers' intents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News domain has volatile preferences and many anonymous users; models should accommodate limited profiling data, short-term preference dynamics, and negative signals. Relevance of readers' intents (why they read) should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypical user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign users to classes (stereotypes) and infer preferences from class prior information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when user background is incomplete. Common stereotypes in NRS: geolocation and habitual patterns. Limitations: cannot learn completely new stereotypes and excessive stereotyping may create segregated groups or filter bubbles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-based user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling users by matching item content features (categories, headlines, sources, topics) extracted via BoW, TF-IDF, Hashing, Word2Vec, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content is similar to previously read items, recommend it. Limitations: traditional methods may not capture semantics and context, and struggle with volatile/time-ordered preferences and anonymous users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative filtering (CF) user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling based on users' interactions; infer preferences from similar users' histories without explicit item analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require item feature analysis but must preserve temporal distinctions in user preferences for NRS (incorporate time sequences) to predict next-news items effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-based user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semantics, ontologies, and external knowledge bases to construct rich content and user profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: OWL ontologies based on IPTC standards, Wikipedia, Microsoft Satori. Applied to incorporate semantic/contextual understanding into recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset types and selection considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of datasets for NRS research: publicly available, proprietary, crawled, synthetic/simulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public benchmarks (Plista, Adressa, Yahoo Webscope, Hacker News, BuzzFeed, MIND) vary in content (timestamp, click logs, reading time, anonymization). Limitations include anonymized article content (features without text), lack of public availability, profanity in social datasets, and task-specific datasets (e.g., fake news datasets may be more suitable for detection than personalization). Researchers often build private crawled datasets due to lack of suitable public datasets.
